title: The Best Savings Plan for U.S. Workers Who Don’t Receive Employer Benefits
description: Building a DIY benefits package: Retirement, Health, and PTO.
content:
Working for a small business, a startup, or as a contractor often means one thing: No Benefits. No 401(k) match, no subsidized health insurance, and no paid time off. While the paycheck might be good, the *net* compensation is lower because you have to fund your own safety net. Workers in this position must become their own HR department. This guide outlines the 'DIY Benefits Stack'—allocating specific percentages of your income to replicate the security of a corporate job.

Key Takeaways

  • The 'Benefit Premium': You must save ~20% more of your income than a corporate employee to match their stability. 10% for retirement (no match) + 10% for healthcare/PTO.
  • The IRA Anchor: Without a 401(k), the IRA (Traditional or Roth) becomes your primary vehicle. Maximize the $7,000 limit every year.
  • Health Savings Account (HSA): If you buy your own insurance on the Marketplace (ACA), choose a High Deductible plan to unlock the HSA. It gives you a tax deduction you desperately need.
  • The 'PTO Fund': If you don't work, you don't get paid. You must save 5% of every paycheck into a 'Vacation/Sick' fund so you can afford to take a week off.

Why It Matters (US Context)

Over 50% of US small business employees do not have access to a retirement plan. The government created the 'myRA' (defunct) and now state-sponsored IRAs (like CalSavers) to help, but the best defense is a personal aggressive savings rate.

Structuring Your DIY Paycheck

When you get paid $4,000, do not spend $4,000. Pretend your salary is lower.

1. Retirement (The Fake 401k)

Corporate workers save 5% and get 5% match (10% total). You get $0 match.
Action: Set up an auto-transfer of 15% of your income to a Brokerage Account or IRA. You have to do the heavy lifting yourself.

2. Health (The Premium)

Corporate workers pay ~$150/mo for insurance; the company pays the rest. You might pay $500/mo.
Action: Treat this as a tax. Use the subsidy calculator on Healthcare.gov to see if you qualify for tax credits.

3. Time Off (The PTO Fund)

2 weeks vacation + 1 week sick = 3 weeks (6% of the year).
Action: Save 6% of every paycheck into a 'Time Off' savings bucket. When you take a vacation, pay yourself from this bucket to cover the lost wages.

Investment Vehicles

  1. Roth IRA: Your first stop. $7,000 limit. Tax-free growth. Flexible withdrawals.
  2. Taxable Brokerage: Since IRAs have low limits ($7k vs $23k 401k), you will need a Taxable account to save enough for retirement. Use tax-efficient ETFs (VTI).
  3. Solo 401(k)? Note: You can only open a Solo 401(k) if you are a contractor (1099). If you are a W-2 employee with no benefits, you cannot open one. You are stuck with IRAs and Brokerage.
  4. Lobby Your Boss: Ask for a 'SIMPLE IRA'. It is very cheap for small businesses to set up and allows them to give you a 3% match.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is a job without benefits worth it?

Only if the salary is 20-30% higher than a job with benefits. If the pay is the same, you are effectively taking a massive pay cut. Do the math.

Can I deduct IRA contributions?

Yes! Since you are not covered by a workplace plan, you can deduct Traditional IRA contributions regardless of how high your income is (no phase-out).

What about disability?

You have no short-term disability coverage. You need a larger emergency fund (6 months) to cover injury or illness.
